name: TB-500

lead: TB-500 is the name used by research-peptide vendors for a synthetic version of thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4) or a fragment of it; the exact molecule sold varies by supplier. Tβ4 itself is a 43-amino-acid protein that is abundant in most human cells and binds actin.

In recovery and looksmaxxing communities it is marketed for tendon, muscle and skin repair, often stacked with BPC-157. The established research on full-length Tβ4 involves wound, eye and cardiac repair; evidence that vendor TB-500 products do the same in healthy people is essentially absent.

paras: Tβ4 sequesters monomeric actin, which influences cell migration, and in animal models it has been linked to angiogenesis, reduced inflammation and improved cell survival in injured tissue. Whether the shorter fragment sold as TB-500 reproduces these effects has not been well established.

Human safety data for the vendor products are lacking, and product identity and purity are inconsistent. Pro-angiogenic activity raises a theoretical concern in people with cancer risk. TB-500 is not an approved drug and is banned by WADA, and a high-profile Australian sports supplement scandal involved thymosin beta-4.

lead: TB-500 is the name used by research-peptide suppliers for a synthetic version of thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4), a small protein found in most human cells, or for a fragment of it. Analytical chemistry work on a veterinary product called TB-500 found its key ingredient to be a short, N-terminally acetylated fragment of Tβ4 covering residues 17 to 23 (Ac-LKKTETQ), the region associated with actin binding, rather than the full-length protein [1][2]. Because the term is used loosely, what a given vendor sells under the name can differ.

In sports-recovery and looksmaxxing communities TB-500 is discussed for tendon, muscle and soft-tissue repair, and is frequently paired with BPC-157. The legitimate research on full-length Tβ4 concerns wound, corneal and cardiac repair; research on the shorter fragment in healthy people recovering from injury is almost absent, and reviews of injectable peptides describe the human evidence for TB-500 as scarce [3][4][5].

TB-500 is not an approved drug. Thymosin beta-4 is prohibited in sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency, and the substance was central to two doping controversies in Australian professional football in the 2010s [6].

paras: Thymosin beta-4 is encoded by the TMSB4X gene and is a major constituent of many cell types, reaching intracellular concentrations as high as 0.5 mM according to Wikipedia. Its best-characterised role is as the principal actin-sequestering protein: it forms a 1:1 complex with globular (G) actin and acts as a buffer for monomeric actin [6]. The sequence LKKTET, beginning at residue 17, is highly conserved among beta-thymosins and is often called the actin-binding motif [6].

A 2012 doping-control paper described a veterinary preparation called TB-500 that contained the peptide LKKTETQ with an artificial N-terminal acetylation, and noted that the preparation was claimed to promote endothelial cell differentiation, angiogenesis and keratinocyte migration [1]. A companion study synthesised the acetylated 17-23 fragment, identified it in TB-500, and described the product as suspected of doping potential [2]. Later reviews group TB-500 (described as a thymosin beta-4 fragment) with Tβ4 itself under a single heading when discussing peptides marketed to athletes [4][5].

TB-500 is promoted in training communities for soft-tissue injuries, tendon and muscle tears and post-surgical recovery, and some posters also hope it may improve skin appearance, such as wrinkles, as part of peptide stacks [7][8][9]. It is typically sold as a research chemical.

Wikipedia reports that full-length Tβ4 has been tested in phase 2 trials in patients with pressure ulcers, venous ulcers and epidermolysis bullosa, where it accelerated repair and was safe and well tolerated, and in trials for dry eye and neurotrophic keratopathy [6]. These trials concerned the protein or an acetylated form used as a medicine, not vendor products labelled TB-500.

Cell-culture and animal experiments have shown that Tβ4 can promote cell migration, blood-vessel formation, stem-cell maturation and cell survival and can lower production of pro-inflammatory cytokines [6]. In mice it has been reported to stimulate formation of new heart muscle cells from precursor cells in the heart's outer lining [6]. Wikipedia notes that these tissue-repair effects may not depend on intracellular actin binding, since the cells affected already have high levels of Tβ4; a role for extracellular receptors has been proposed [6].

An oxidised form, Tβ4 sulfoxide, was reported by a Glasgow group in 1999 to show anti-inflammatory effects on neutrophils [6]. Whether the shorter fragment sold as TB-500 reproduces the effects of the full protein has not been established in the sources reviewed. Orthopaedic reviews list TB-500, BPC-157 and GHK-Cu together as wound-healing peptides that act on angiogenesis, matrix remodelling and fibroblast activation, while noting a lack of clinical trials [10].

Reviews aimed at sports-medicine clinicians conclude that many unapproved peptides show favourable tissue-repair and metabolic outcomes in animals but that rigorous human safety data are scarce [4]. A 2026 primer for orthopaedic physicians evaluated BPC-157, Tβ4, TB-500 and other peptides and reported that findings were largely unvalidated in human trials [3]. A further 2026 review in the American Journal of Sports Medicine states that peptides in this group are often perceived as low risk despite an absence of efficacy or safety data for many of them [11].

A 2026 histopathological and biomechanical study in rats examined BPC-157 and TB-500 together in Achilles tendon healing [12]; its details were not available in the abstract reviewed. The wider literature on Tβ4 in animals, summarised in older reviews, describes it as a multifunctional repair and regeneration peptide [13][14].

No completed, published controlled trial of TB-500 for tendon, muscle or appearance outcomes in healthy or injured people was identified in the sources reviewed. A review of the field describes only preclinical data for the popular recovery peptides apart from small human case series [3][10].

One trial of the fragment is registered: NCT07487363, a phase 1/2 study of TB-500 (thymosin beta-4 17-23 fragment) for cardiovascular biomarkers in people with stable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (n=80), listed as recruiting from February 2026 [15]. Separate human trials exist for full-length thymosin beta-4, as noted above [6][16].

There are no systematic human safety data for vendor TB-500 products. A 2026 review of 'biohacking' injectables lists BPC-157, TB-500 and melanotan-II among unapproved peptides that lack established human safety profiles and describes potential risks including product contamination, impurities, inaccurate dosing, pathological angiogenesis and carcinogenesis [5]. A review of approved and unapproved peptide therapies similarly states that there is potential for serious harm because rigorous human safety data are scarce [4].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, notes that Tβ4 has been correlated with tumour metastatic potential and angiogenesis in some cancers, a dual role it describes as a reason for caution in regenerative use [17]. The relevance of this to TB-500 products has not been tested in humans.

Wikipedia states that thymosin beta-4 is considered performance-enhancing and is banned by WADA because it may aid soft-tissue recovery and allow higher training loads [6]. It featured in two Australian controversies in which large numbers of players at the Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks (National Rugby League) and the Essendon Football Club (Australian Football League) were found to have been administered the substance in a programme organised by the sports scientist Stephen Dank, and were suspended [6].

Analytical chemists developed detection methods for TB-500 in horse urine and plasma from 2012 onwards, and later papers examined analytical issues such as adsorption losses of TB-500 during sample handling [1][2][18]. A review of doping-control analysis lists TB-500 among the peptides that testing laboratories must cover [19].

Thymosins were studied from the early 1960s as thymus-derived factors with immune effects, and Allan Goldstein's group prepared a partially purified calf thymus extract called thymosin fraction 5 in 1972, according to Grokipedia [17]. Wikipedia notes that thymosin beta-4 was the second peptide from this fraction to be fully sequenced and synthesised, after thymosin alpha-1, and that it was first thought to be a thymic hormone before being shown to be an actin-sequestering protein [6].

Reviews published in 2005 and 2010 framed Tβ4 as an actin-sequestering protein that 'moonlights' in tissue repair, setting the scientific background to later commercial interest [13][14]. The veterinary TB-500 preparation emerged in racehorse doping-control literature by 2012 [1].

On T Nation, TB-500 is almost always mentioned alongside BPC-157, in logs where lifters describe injecting both near an injured hamstring, knee or shoulder [7][8][20]. Some posters list the two peptides among large stacks that also include anabolic steroids, growth hormone and other drugs [8]. One forum poster notes that a 'research chemical' defence might not protect someone prosecuted for possession of TB-500, with used needles as evidence [21].
